COMMENTS FROM THE EDITORS
Time to Abandon NASH?
T
he name of a liver disease should encapsulate the
key characteristic of the disease. In two or three
words, it should reﬂect the pathophysiology
mechanism and clinical presentation. Chronic hepatitis
C is, in this sense, unambiguously clear, although this
was not always the case. Who remembers that chronic
viral hepatitis was named “serum jaundice” when
Dame Sheila Sherlock began her career in hepatology?
The name of a disease should evolve as it is better
diagnosed and better understood. “Primary biliary
cirrhosis” was an adequate name in the twentieth cen-
tury but not anymore in the twenty-ﬁrst when most
of the patients do not have cirrhosis at the time of
diagnosis. This is confusing and stressful for patients.
This has been recognized and addressed with the sug-
gestion of a new name, “primary biliary cholangitis,”
which elegantly keeps the acronym “PBC.” Even the
name “cirrhosis” can be challenged in the context of
patient management. Cirrhosis is deﬁned by rigid
pathology criteria. It becomes more and more evident
that there is a gradual transition from advanced ﬁbro-
sis into cirrhosis and that cirrhosis has different clini-
cal stages. The term “cirrhosis” will not disappear, but
the dynamic of the clinical context should be reﬂected
in the disease name.
Presently,
in
hepatology,
the
worst
name
is
“nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).” It sounds good
and is easy to say in many languages. It is very conven-
ient as it captures the concepts of accumulation of fat in
the liver and parenchymal inﬂammation and excludes
alcohol, but this name is undermined by major limita-
tions. It is notoriously difﬁcult to have a reliable anam-
nesis
of
alcohol
intake.
Sensitivity
to
alcohol
is
individual. Worse still, the combination of alcohol expo-
sure with metabolic liver disease induced by obesity and
diabetes is extremely frequent in daily practice and leads
to contradictory diagnoses like NASH/alcoholic steato-
hepatitis. The steatosis can be assessed noninvasively,
whereas ballooning and inﬂammation require a liver
biopsy. This is the gold standard but a weak gold stand-
ard. Sampling variability is signiﬁcant, as shown by Rat-
ziu et al.1 The interpretation of the histology is based on
an appreciation made by the pathologist. The scoring
system of Kleiner et al. is useful to grade the pathologic
ﬁndings, but the authors were prudent not to give a
diagnostic cutoff.2 The interpretation of the histology
has improved with the introduction of the fatty liver
inhibition of progression (FLIP) scoring system, which
is diagnostic.3 However, in the case of NASH-induced
cirrhosis the pathologic features vanish, thus rendering
histologic diagnosis obsolete.
The acronym “NASH” is so imperfect that it should
be replaced, but the question is, what should replace it?
The search of a better name highlights how much more
needs to be done in the ﬁeld. One can consider meta-
bolic disease–induced liver injury (MILI), an acronym
in line with other diagnoses in hepatology like DILI
(drug-induced liver injury). However, many other well-
deﬁned liver diseases, glycogenosis to mention one
example, qualify as MILI. We can narrow it down to
insulin resistance–induced liver injury (IRILI), which
retains what is believed to be the main pathophysiologic
mechanism in NASH. However, it excludes NASH
driven by genetic alteration like mutation in the
PNPLA3
gene.4
These
considerations
reveal
how
NASH is heterogeneous and includes different diseases.
In the end what we need is positive diagnostic, noninva-
sive
tests
based
on
pathophysiologic
mechanisms.
Metabolite signatures have already been explored and
seem a very appealing area.5 Modiﬁcation of proteins
that reﬂect changes in metabolism might also be of
interest.6 To validate these tests, researchers need access
to prospective cohorts of well-characterized patients.
Many liver units around the world are dedicating
resources to gather systematic data and sample acquisi-
tion. Then, collaborative multicenter projects have to be
put in place and coordinated like the NASH Clinical
Research Network in North America and the European
consortium FLIP, which have both made important con-
tributions to the ﬁeld in recent years.
The days of the disease name “NASH” are numbered.
It will be replaced when positive noninvasive tests based
on the pathophysiologic mechanisms become available

that happens in the near future.
